name: Badrinath Temple
summary: The Himalayan Vishnu dham of the Char Dham circuit, open seasonally, with deep ties to Adi Shankaracharya’s tradition.
mythology: Badrinath is the Himalayan Vishnu seat of Adi Shankaracharya’s Char Dham and also belongs to the Uttarakhand Chota Char Dham. Classical tradition associates the site with Nar-Narayan meditation and Vishnu’s presence in the Badri forest. Shankaracharya’s digvijaya narratives credit him with establishing the living pilgrimage and monastic order connected to the shrine.
scriptureLinks: Accounts summarised from widely cited Puranic, epic, and pilgrimage traditions; local tellings may differ.
festivals: Closing for winter (deity moves to Joshimath)
bestTime: May–June and September–October. Closed in deep winter.
whatToCarry: Woolens, rain protection, altitude awareness meds if advised by your doctor, ID, offline maps.
climate: High-altitude cold; sudden weather shifts common.
nearestRail: Rishikesh / Haridwar, then long road journey via Joshimath.
nearestAirport: Dehradun; limited helicopter options in Char Dham season.
accommodation: Temple committee and GMVN rooms, plus private hotels in Badrinath town — book ahead in peak season.
localFood: Simple vegetarian Garhwali / North Indian pilgrim food; prasadam.
otherFood: Limited; stick to sealed water and busy kitchens at altitude.
dressCode: Warm modest clothing. Footwear off in temple. No South-Indian-style dhoti mandate.
darshanTimings: Seasonal schedule with morning and evening aartis. Winter worship continues at Joshimath.
specialEntry: Online / counter systems vary by year under temple committee rules.
restrictions: Respect plastic bans and fragile mountain ecology. Follow VIP / queue notices only from official counters.
lockers: Small cloak facilities near temple approaches; travel light.

disclaimer: Opening/closing dates and road status change yearly — confirm before booking.

localBeliefs:
Garhwal belief holds that the deity ‘resides’ at Badrinath in the open season and moves to Joshimath for winter worship — a seasonal theology shared with other high Himalayan dhams. Mana village, Vyas Gufa, and related spots are woven into local Mahabharata and sage lore.

Pilgrims often combine Badrinath with Kedarnath, treating the dual Vishnu–Shiva Himalayan yatra as a complete spiritual circuit.
